title: Ruptured Globe & Open Globe Injuries (OGI): Master Clinical Infographic
summary: A ruptured globe represents a sight-threatening ophthalmologic emergency defined as a full-thickness breach of the cornea, sclera, or both caused by blunt trauma. Immediate structural preservation, rigid eye shielding, urgent CT orbit, broad-spectrum endophthalmitis prophylaxis, and meticulous primary surgical exploration are essential to salvage visual potential.

sections.title: Anatomical Predilection Sites for Blunt Rupture

branches: Corneoscleral Limbus (Abrupt transition in tissue architecture)
Prior Surgical Scars (PKP graft margin, Cataract incision, Trabeculectomy)
Anterior Segment: Corectopia pointing to wound, peaked pupil, shallow/flat or abnormally deep AC, iris prolapse
Subconjunctival Signs: 360° elevated chemosis, bullous subconjunctival hemorrhage ('bull's eye')
IOP Discrepancy: Marked ocular hypotony (IOP < 5 mmHg), though normal/high IOP does NOT rule out rupture
Posterior Segment: Vitreous hemorrhage, lack of red reflex, commotio retinae, avulsion of optic nerve
Vision & Motility: Profound drop in visual acuity (often Light Perception or Hand Motion), marked duction deficits

sections.title: Emergency Room Initial Stabilization Protocol
content: Immediate Fox Shield: Place rigid eye shield resting on orbital bones; zero external pressure on the globe.
Strict NPO & Tetanus: Keep patient strictly NPO for urgent surgical exploration; update tetanus toxoid.
Antiemetics & Analgesia: IV Ondansetron (4-8 mg) to prevent vomiting/Valsalva; IV analgesia as needed.
Systemic Prophylactic Antibiotics: IV Vancomycin (1 g q12h) + IV Ceftazidime (2 g q8h) OR Oral Moxifloxacin (400 mg daily).
Non-Contrast CT Orbits: Thin axial/coronal cuts (1.0 mm) to detect IOFBs, scleral step-offs, and orbital fractures.
Transfer to OR: Urgent primary wound closure within 12-24 hours to reduce endophthalmitis and PVR risks.

sections.title: Absolute Contraindications & Red Flags
content: NEVER apply direct external pressure on the globe or place a pressure patch.
NEVER perform Goldmann applanation tonometry, gonioscopy, or scleral depression.
NEVER instill preservative-containing, viscous, or irritating topical drops (e.g., cyclopentolate/phenylephrine).
NEVER order an MRI if a metallic foreign body has not been definitively ruled out by CT.
NEVER perform contact B-scan ultrasonography with excessive probe force over an open eye.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis of Severe Ocular Trauma

rows: Peaked pupil, scleral contour disruption, collapsed globe ('flat tire' sign) on CT
Severe proptosis, tight orbit/eyelids, optic nerve compromise, tenting of posterior globe
Intact corneoscleral shell, erythrocyte layering in AC, round reactive pupil
Elevated secondary to episcleral venous pressure
Pulsatile proptosis, corkscrew episcleral vessels, orbital bruit, enlarged SOV on CT
Disinsertion of iris root from ciliary body, widened ciliary body band, intact eyewall

sections.title: Step-by-Step Surgical Repair Technique
content: 1. Anesthesia Induction: General anesthesia with rapid-sequence intubation avoiding depolarizing agents (e.g., succinylcholine) to prevent extrusion of intraocular contents.
2. Conjunctival Peritomy & Exploration: Perform a 360° limbal peritomy with relaxing radial incisions; gently isolate the four rectus muscles using vessel loops without traction.
3. Corneal & Limbal Restoration: Re-approximate the limbus first using 9-0 or 10-0 nylon cardinal sutures to restore primary anatomical landmarks.
4. Cornea Wound Closure: Suture clear corneal lacerations with 10-0 nylon using short, deep (90% thickness) interrupted sutures, burying all knots towards the wound.
5. Management of Prolapsed Uvea: Reposit viable, clean iris/ciliary tissue if presenting within 24 hours; excise necrotic, non-viable, or grossly contaminated uveal tissue.
6. Scleral Laceration Repair: Repair sclera moving 'anterior-to-posterior' ('close-as-you-go' technique) using 8-0 or 9-0 nylon/vicryl interrupted sutures.
7. Exploration Under Rectus Muscles: Carefully inspect underneath all muscle insertions where rupture commonly extends; avoid excessive globe manipulation.

content.explanation: P: Protect with rigid Fox shield (NO patch) | R: Radiographic CT orbits (thin cuts, NO MRI initially) | O: Operative primary closure within 24 hours | T: Tetanus update & broad-spectrum IV antibiotics | E: Examine pupil for corectopia/peaking | C: Control emesis and pain to prevent Valsalva | T: Tonometry/gonioscopy are strictly CONTRAINDICATED.

branches: Endophthalmitis (3-10% incidence; highest with soil contamination/IOFB)
Sympathetic Ophthalmia (Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis; peak at 2-12 weeks)
Traumatic Glaucoma (Angle recession, hemolytic, or epithelial downgrowth)
Phthisis Bulbi & Loss of Eye Architecture

sections.title: Sympathetic Ophthalmia (SO): High-Yield Facts
content: Pathophysiology: Cell-mediated autoimmune response directed against retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and uveal melanocytes unmasked by trauma.
Incidence & Timing: Rare (< 0.5% of open globe trauma); 80% occur within 3 months, 90% within 1 year of inciting injury (rarely before 2 weeks).
Hallmark Histopathology: Diffuse non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the uveal tract with Dalén-Fuchs nodules (epithelioid cells under RPE); choriocapillaris is classically spared.
Clinical Presentation: Bilateral mutton-fat keratic precipitates, vitritis, choroidal thickening, exudative retinal detachments, papillitis.
Prevention & Enucleation: Primary enucleation/evisceration of a blind, severely traumatized eye within 14 days eliminates the risk of SO in the fellow eye.

sections.title: Landmark Trials & Evidence-Based Guidelines
content: Ocular Trauma Score (OTS Study - Kuhn et al.): Established the gold-standard predictive model for final visual outcome based on initial VA, presence of rupture, RD, APD, and endophthalmitis.

Timing of Vitrectomy for Post-Traumatic Vitreoretinal Pathology: Delayed secondary vitrectomy at 7-14 days allows posterior vitreous detachment to develop and reduces intraoperative bleeding risk, compared to immediate vitrectomy.

Endophthalmitis Prophylaxis in Trauma (Essex et al.): Prophylactic systemic fluoroquinolones or IV Vancomycin/Ceftazidime significantly lowers infectious endophthalmitis rates, especially when administered < 24 hours from injury.
